w: Hamburg's self-declared 'sinful mile' runs straight through St. Pauli as the city's biggest red-light district and one of its two nightlife hearts. Locals just call it the Kiez, and each year the Reeperbahn Festival turns the whole strip into one of Europe's largest club festivals.
s: The 'sinful mile' at the heart of St. Pauli nightlife
_facts: Street and entertainment district in St. Pauli, one of Hamburg's two nightlife centres (the other being Sternschanze), the city's major red-light district
Nicknamed die sundige Meile (the sinful mile) and Kiez; the Reeperbahn Festival is among the largest club festivals

w: A glass wave rises off a 1963 brick warehouse in HafenCity - Herzog & de Meuron's design for Hamburg's tallest inhabited building, 108 metres up. It took a private couple's initiative to get it built at all; it opened in January 2017 with a light show and the NDR Elbphilharmonie Orchestra.
s: A glass wave atop a 1960s brick warehouse
_facts: Concert hall in HafenCity built atop the 1963 brick warehouse Kaispeicher A, designed by Herzog & de Meuron, Hamburg's tallest inhabited building at 108 metres
Result of a private initiative by architect/developer Alexander Gerard and art historian Jana Marko; officially inaugurated 11 January 2017 with a light show and the NDR Elbphilharmonie Orchestra

w: Briefly the tallest building on Earth when George Gilbert Scott finished rebuilding it in 1874, St. Nicholas was gutted by Allied bombing in the Second World War and never restored. The bell-filled spire and crypt still stand as a memorial - ride the 2005 lift to a platform 75 metres up for the view over what's left.
s: Once the world's tallest building, now a war memorial
_facts: Gothic Revival former Hauptkirche, rebuilt by 1874 to a George Gilbert Scott design and was briefly the tallest building in the world (1874-1876)
Destroyed by WWII bombing raids, leaving only crypt, tower and site as a memorial; a lift installed in 2005 reaches a platform 75.3 metres up

w: Fritz Höger's 1924 office block slices through Fischertwiete like the prow of a ship, its sharp brick angles turning the whole Kontorhaus District into a showcase of 1920s Brick Expressionism. UNESCO added it to the World Heritage list in 2015 - a working office building that still doubles as a monument.
s: A ship's prow in brick, UNESCO-listed since 2015
_facts: Ten-story office building in the Kontorhaus District, 1920s Brick Expressionism style, designed by Fritz Hoger, finished 1924, spans Fischertwiete Street
Inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 as part of the Kontorhaus District
